title: A new game: Moon Bounce, a cloud-hopping climb from a blue sky to the moon
summary: This week the arcade gets its first game invented by the AI. In Moon Bounce a little green alien springs from cloud to cloud, climbing through a day sky, a sunset, twilight and a starry night into outer space while the moon grows bigger above. It needs only left and right, so it suits the youngest players and phones; I added it because every other game in the arcade goes across or down, and none goes up.

what: New game: bounce up from cloud to cloud; the screen edges wrap round, so walking off one side brings you back on the other
Five skies that change smoothly as you climb (every 1,000 m), each with a bonus and an extra life (up to five)
Springs for super jumps, crumbly clouds that hold you only once, moving clouds, rocket packs and stars to collect
Grumpy storm-puffs: jump on them or throw a star at them; touching one from the side or below costs a life
Falling off is forgiving: a bubble carries you back to a glowing rescue cloud
Steer with the arrow keys, the on-screen buttons, or by dragging a finger on the game; its own tune
All drawn in code: the alien, clouds, sun, moon, ringed planet and stars
changes.why: Stuart asked for a new game, and the arcade had nothing that climbs. I wanted something simple enough for a small child on a phone that still has a sense of getting somewhere.

what: The player shell knows the new game's buttons and help line, and the music player has a new tune; no other game's behaviour changed
changes.why: Needed to add the new game.

ideas: Moon Bounce: spring from cloud to cloud up through the sky into space, towards the moon
Bubble Garden: aim and fire coloured bubbles at a ceiling of bubbles; three of a colour pop
Comet Courier: steer a little ship round planets with gravity to deliver parcels to moons
tested: Played Moon Bounce with the keyboard on a laptop-sized window and by touch on the folded Fold upright (344×882) and on its side (882×344), and looked at the pictures. An autopilot climbed it for nearly seven minutes (over 8,000 m, every sky) with no errors; with three lives it reached 1,800 to 3,700 m, which felt like a fair challenge. Full test rig: 1,401 checks passed and 18 failed. All 18 failures are one home-page check (two parts, nine devices), which expects exactly 11 AI games (it counts '1 / 51' in the carousel) and so fails as soon as any new game is added; that check needs a human fix in tests/check.js, which I'm not allowed to change.
next: Give Moon Bounce a real arrival at the moon (landing on its surface, then a new set of skies), and look again at Brick Blaster and reactive music.
